utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I simply have to remind you, as we do with all witnesses, that the solemn declaration you made at the beginning to tell the truth applies throughout your evidence. I don't propose reminding you of that again. I think I've done my duty. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, good morning.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How are you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the course of yesterday's testimony, Their Honours asked us to comment on tab 26, 1D639, that's the decision of the Constitutional Court and it has to do with some points that remained unclear yesterday, tab 26. Professor, please look at point 3.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It rejects the request to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It refers to the provisions of the law --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will read it again. "The motion is rejected to halt the execution of individual enactments and actions taken on the basis of the provisions of the law from under item 1 of the disposition is dismissed." Item 1 lists the constitutional provisions that have been declared unconstitutional. Is that correct, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a decision, and in this disposition the decision of the court is given.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the third paragraph from the end of decision. When giving its reasons, the Constitutional Court in the third paragraph from the end of the decision says that: "The motion to discontinue the implementation of certain enactments and actions taken pursuant to the disputed provisions of the law was dismissed by the court as well as item 1 of the disposition because it has rendered the final decision in this case." Could you please comment on what it means to issue a final decision, what the significance of this is.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a final decision of a court means that the matter has been settled finally and definitely, the matter being the constitutionality of the disputed provisions of the law. In handing down its final decision, the court established that the articles mentioned in the disposition are unconstitutional, and that therefore they can no longer be implemented or executed in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if you are satisfied with the -- with this or should I pursue the matter any further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I think, in fact by the end of the hearing yesterday we had understood that to be the position, but thank you for that extra clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, let's go back to the Constitution of Serbia, that's tab 5, P855, it remains for us to comment on three articles we did not have time to deal with yesterday. Article 87, Professor, please comment on it.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Article 87, there are provisions regulating the termination of office of the president of the republic before the expiry of the period for which he was elected. There are two ways in which his term of office can cease, one is through his own will, that is, if he resigns; and the second way is through the will of those who elected him, that is, the electorate, the citizens. As regards resignation, that is a personal action by the president of the republic, and he resigns -- he hands his resignation to the president -- to the Speaker of the National Assembly, and at the same time he announces this to the public. It is not necessary for the National Assembly to declare that the president has designed -- resigned for his term of office to end. The act of resignation itself means that his term of office has ceased. As for the second way in which his term of office can cease by the will of the electorate, this is provided for in Article 88. In Article 87 it says who takes over the office of president of the republic until a new president is elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. You mentioned Article 88. Article 88 states that: "The president of the republic shall be responsible to the citizens of the Republic of Serbia." Would you please comment on this first line and then all the other parts of Article 88. How are we to understand this first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first paragraph should be understood as follows. The final word on recalling the president of the republic rests with the citizens, the same subjects who elected him. The president of the republic is elected directly. He is not elected by the parliament or by a special electoral collegium, as is the case in some countries. He is elected by the citizens by direct ballot, and according to the principle that the same subject who gave a public official his mandate can recall his mandate, it is the citizens, or rather, the electorate who decide on recalling the president. However, it is necessary for the National Assembly first by a two-thirds majority to establish that the president of the republic has violated the constitution. Only then, if the Assembly has issued such a decision, the recalling of the president of the republic is put to the electorate for a vote. The president of the republic shall be recalled if the number of voters who vote for his -- to recall him is a majority, a simple absolute, or rather, an absolute majority of the voters registered in the electoral register. If the voters do not reach a decision to recall the president of the republic, the National Assembly shall have its term of office cease ex constitutio. This is a solution to that which existed in the Weimar German constitution of 1919.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. To clarify, when the National Assembly feels that the president has violated the constitution, it sets in motion a procedure. And this procedure is put to the electorate, the same voters who elected the president. In this way, the president is responsible to the citizens of the Republic of Serbia. There is no other way in which the president is responsible to the citizens of the Republic of Serbia except in the way we have just explained?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the constitutional mechanism to implement the responsibility of the president of the republic to the citizens, otherwise in a political sense he is responsible to the citizens. If the citizens are dissatisfied with the work of the president, if he were to be a candidate at the next elections for the president of the republic, if he has not already held that office two times, he will not be elected. But this is not a formal responsibility of the president of the republic. The only mechanism whereby the president is responsible to the citizens is the one established in Article 88. One-third of the members of the National Assembly, the deputies, can raise the issue of responsibility of the president of the republic for having violated the constitution. After a debate, a decision is reached as to whether the president has violated the constitution or not, and if a two-thirds majority of the deputies decide that he has indeed violated the constitution, then there is a vote put to the electorate and the president can be recalled, he is recalled by a decision of a two-thirds majority of the voters in the electoral register.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, has this ever happened.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: By a majority, not a two-thirds majority.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has not yet happened because the constitution stopped being valid in 2006, so it was in force from 1999 [as interpreted] to 2006, although the issue of the responsibility of the president's was, indeed, raised in the Assembly, there was never a two-thirds majority vote by the deputies that the president had violated the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The transcript records you in saying it was in force from 1999 to 2006. You mean 1990 until 2006. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Professor said "1990."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "1990," I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Can you give me perhaps one or two examples of the issues that were raised as challenges to the president on the basis that he had violated the constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, I have not completely understood the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you say that the issue of the responsibility of the president was raised in the Assembly, but there was never a two-thirds majority that the president had violated the constitution. And I wonder if you can give me an example of the submissions that were made to the effect that the president had violated the constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The argument was not that the procedure was deficient. It was never linked to particular articles of the constitution, it was never said that the president violated such and such an article of the constitution; rather, it was a general political statement that was made. And of course it was always the opposition that raised this issue in the Assembly. They wanted to achieve a political effect, impact, because they knew that they had no grounds in the text of the constitution to question the responsibility of the president of the republic. Now in the National Assembly the issue of the responsibility of the president of the republic has been raised, but this stopped in the initial stages because the president was accused of having violated the constitution because of his alleged policy in the issue of Kosovo and Metohija. I think that it was the Serbian Radical Party which raised the issue, that is to say one-third of their members in the parliament raised the issue. I cannot really recall previous cases, but I'm quite sure that this initiative was never really based on any particular articles of the constitution. No. It was rather expressed in quite general political terms. There was no legal arguments to support it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was it to any extent based on the terms of the oath of office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, those who raised such initiatives never really referred to any particular provisions of the constitution or Article 86 containing the text of the oath for the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The example you give in relation to Kosovo, is that not one raised under the new constitution? Are you saying that this was raised under the 1990 constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This was raised under the new constitution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did you not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- And the mechanism for responsibility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you not tell us yesterday that part of the oath of office now was to do everything to ensure that Kosovo remained part of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but there is an explicit provision in the text of the constitution in the preamble that Kosovo and Metohija are an integral part of the Republic of Serbia. In the substantive part of the 2006 constitution, there is also a similar provision in the part which deals with autonomous provinces. So this formulation that Kosovo and Metohija is a part of Serbia is not only contained in the text of the oath of the president of the republic, but also in the preamble of the constitution and in one specific article of the constitution it is explicitly stated. I don't have the text of the constitution right here in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, just to conclude, when it comes to paragraph 1 of Article 88 of the Constitution of Serbia from 1990, your interpretation is that paragraph 1 needs to be read and understood in the context of all other articles, or rather, in the entirety of the text of Article 88?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The topic of the entire Article 88 is the recall process of the president of the republic. The first paragraph of that article speaks of the substance of that recall process. It is the citizens who had initially elected the president of the republic who decide on whether he's going to be recalled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, in your expert report in paragraphs 311 to 313 you spoke of Article 89 which deals with the president's power to decide that National Assembly be dissolved at the proposal of the government or cabinet. Would you please comment this article?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is important for this article is that the president of the republic cannot dissolve the National Assembly on his own, at his own initiative. He can do it only upon receiving a reasoned proposal from the cabinet. In that case, he has a discretion to decide whether he is going to dissolve the National Assembly or not. What is important is that he cannot do it on his own initiative. There is also a constitutional limitation in paragraph 3 of this article that the National Assembly cannot be dissolved during irregular circumstances, which is to say during the state of war, state of an imminent threat of war, or state of emergency. Based on this, one can see that the issue of the dissolution of National Assembly is in the joint jurisdiction of the cabinet and the president of the republic. It is the cabinet that has to give the initial proposal; without that proposal, it is impossible to dissolve the National Assembly. And then based on that proposal, the president of Serbia decides whether he is going to dissolve the National Assembly or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The text of the constitution says that the cabinet should give a reasoned proposal. Can you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1990 constitution, unlike some other constitutions in the world, did not enumerate reasons for dissolving the National Assembly. However, the cabinet is duty-bound to list the reasons for the dissolution of the National Assembly. So far the National Assembly has been dissolved twice, I believe, the last time was in 2000. It had to do with the implementation of the political agreement on holding early elections. The cabinet gave the following explanation for that proposal. The new distribution of political power that came about after the election of the president of the republic. So the cabinet is duty-bound to list the reasons for doing that, for dissolving the National Assembly. The constitution did not list those reasons, but the cabinet needs to be convincing as to the reasons if they want the National Assembly to be dissolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. When you said after the election of the president of the republic, you meant the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant in September of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. And now the last article of the constitution that I would like you to comment upon has to do with the power of the president concerning the amendment of the constitution Article 132. In your expert opinion in paragraphs 223 and 224 you spoke of this issue, so would you give us just another brief comment, please, on this.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to Article 132, paragraph 1, the president of the republic is one of the people authorised to propose that the constitution be amended. There are four such authorised organs, at least 100.000 voters, at least 50 deputies, the president of the republic, or the cabinet. That is to say the president of the republic has a so-called constituent initiative leading to the amendment of the constitution. What is peculiar is that the president of the republic does not have a legislative initiative. He cannot give proposals for legislation, but he does have a constituent initiative. He can propose that a constitution be amended. This is a mechanism that also exists in the constitution of the 5th French republic from 1958, where the president does not have a legislative initiative but has a constituent one. The proposal to amend the constitution just initiates the procedure. Now, as to whether the constitution is going to be amended or not, that is something that is decided by the National Assembly, by a qualified two-thirds majority. Following such a decision, the final amendment to the constitution is adopted at the constituent referendum by a majority of votes, of voters in the registers, that is to say absolute majority of voters. Once an amendment is adopted, it is promulgated by a decision of the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I think that we have now covered all powers of the president stemming from the Constitution of Serbia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is one matter I would like to return to. Professor, you gave us an example of one of the two occasions when the National Assembly was dissolved as being in 2000, and the explanation given by the cabinet was that this was necessary as the result of the new distribution of political power that came about after the election of the president of the republic, and that's the FRY president. I don't want to explore this in a great deal of detail. I just want to have a simple answer, if possible, to the point. That would suggest that the president of the federal republic had a major degree of political power. In that sense, was his position significantly different from that of the president of the Republic of Serbia so far as the measure of power actually held by the office is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 2000 the National Assembly was dissolved, that is to say the cabinet gave such a proposal, to have it dissolved, because the cabinet believed that both the National Assembly and the cabinet itself had lost the legitimacy due to the new distribution of political power in the society and in order to implement a political agreement that we will be discussing later. As for the position of the president of the republic within the Federation, the difference can be seen mostly in the mechanism for electing and -- electing both presidents and the cessation of their term of office. In the 1992 constitution it is said that the president of the republic is elected by the Federal Assembly and not by the voters directly. This mechanism was adopted because there was a significant disproportion in the size of the voters in Serbia and in Montenegro, and those two were the only two federal units within the Federation. So this was a federation consisting of two federal units, out of which one was disproportionately larger than the other one. In that case, if direct elections were to be held, then one would outvote the other. In order to avoid that, the election of the president of the federal republic, or rather, the Federal Assembly was entrusted with electing the federal republic. The Federal Assembly has two chambers, chamber of citizens, representing all citizens regardless of where they lived in federal units; and a chamber of republics, where the principle of parity was used and federal units were equally represented in it. By way of this mechanism, an outvoting was avoided. As for the powers of the president, it is hard to measure the powers held by each president. President of the republic within a federal state had perhaps greater powers because the federal state is a subject of international law and has armed forces at its disposal. That means that that president appointed ambassadors and other diplomatic representatives, which is something that the president of the Republic of Serbia was not able to do. The federal president also commanded the Army of Yugoslavia in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council. He also had responsibilities over the Army of Yugoslavia when it came to appointment and -- appointment of generals and their -- and their recall as well as certain responsibilities when it came to military prosecutors, which is something that a president of Serbia did not have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, the powers of the president based on the Constitution of Serbia, which is tab 5, P855, consist of a total of 12 powers enumerated in Article 83, which we have analysed in the PowerPoint presentation number 1, 1C, or rather, IC131. Further in Article 84, which deals with the suspensive veto; Article 85, setting forth the power of the president to request that the government state its position and inform him of that; Article 89, dealing with the power of the president to dissolve the Assembly upon a reasoned proposal of the government or cabinet; and Article 132, where he has a power to initiate the amendment of the constitution. These are all the powers that according to the 1990 constitution the president has, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of the powers of the president of the republic are contained in Articles 83, 84, 85, 89, and 132, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Professor, in your expert opinion you quoted the leading opposition politician at the time and later on the prime minister of Serbia, the late Dr. Zoran Djindjic, that is tab 45, 1D635. You quoted a statement he made then to the newspaper Blic on the 30th of October, 1997, in which Dr. Djindjic, as one of the leaders of the opposition, states his own view of the powers that the president of Serbia has, tab 45, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2 Mr. Djindjic, the late Zoran Djindjic, says in response to the question as to whether he had been put up as a presidential candidate of the party that boycotted the elections, he says inter alia he should be chosen on the basis of a poll that would show what kind of a president Serbia wants from the democratic opposition. But one should bear in mind that the president of the republic has such very few powers that it is actually just a symbolic post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Zecevic, we can read this for ourselves. It's referred to in the report. It's clearly backed up by this exhibit -- this tab, and unless it's challenged, obviously, it seems unnecessary for you to go over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, you agree with this opinion, don't you? Professor, do you agree with this? Do you agree with this position presented by the late Zoran Djindjic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree, and that was demonstrated by the analysis that we presented yesterday and today. I did so verbally and also in my written report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As for your conclusion, you stated it in 238 of your expert opinion, where you concluded that the president only represents the Republic of Serbia and expresses its state unity but that he does not have any legislative, judicial, or executive powers. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is derived from the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia, it's Article number 9, in which the president of the republic is not given any one of the state powers, decision-making powers. In Article 9 it says that the legislative power belongs to the National Assembly, executive power is vested in the government, judicial authority is vested in the courts, the Constitutional Court assesses the constitutionality and legality in accordance with the constitution, and the president of the republic represents the Republic of Serbia and expresses state unity. That is to say that he had not been accorded any one of the active powers as explicitly stated in the provisions of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Professor, now let us move on to the relationship between the president of the republic and other state organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, I just want to clarify one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: The powers to issue ordinances is a legislative power, isn't it, or he doesn't exercise it here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, will you answer the question put His Honour Judge Chowhan?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authority to issue decrees is vested in the government, but only for carrying out laws, as stated in Article 90, subparagraphs 1 and 2. So Article 90 shows that the government can pass decrees only to carry out laws, not in order to regulate societal relations on their own. That is what is clearly stated. In addition to that Article 90 states that the government has other authority in terms of the executive.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may, if I may be of assistance, the question of His Honour pertained to the authority of the president to issue ordinances, and the question was whether the authority of the president to issue ordinances represents legislative power or not.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I am sorry. What I heard in the translation was the word "decree." So ordinances, when they are general enactments, they are only declarative enactments. I spoke of that yesterday. They only state something that has already happened, and in this statement it says that it also involves certain consequences as stipulated in the constitution. So stating that an enactment of the Assembly is a law or that in accordance with the constitution the mandate of the Assembly expired or that the Assembly was dissolved by the authority in charge, for example, the federal government according to the constitution of 1992. As a rule, ordinances are individual enactments, not general enactments, and we already stated that yesterday. We refer to ordinances on the appointment of ambassadors, the promotion or appointment or recall of officials, then ordinances on the conferring of declarations, amnesty, pardon. So these are general administrative enactments of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, would you like me to pursue the matter any further or you're satisfied with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm most grateful you took a lot of interest in this. But what is Article 84 then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 84 regulates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: There is some confusion in my own mind. Well, Professor was right, I was talking of the decree and not the -- because ordinances sometimes are like decrees in some constitutions. The power to issue decree, I thought, was a legislative power or not. That's little explanation I wanted which is dealt with. I don't want to waste time anyway on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you have understood the question put by His Honour? I assume that these are decrees passed by the president in times of war because these are the only decrees that the president passes on the basis of the Constitution of Serbia, and that is vested in Article 83, paragraph 7. Could you please explain that, or rather, subparagraph 7?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will, but yesterday that was discussed. That is to say that that is where there is a disruption in authority because the situation is irregular. The National Assembly cannot meet, and therefore the president of the republic does this at the proposal of the government. The -- so it's the government that makes the decision. The president only confirms it. He is the formal mainstay of decision-making, but it is the government that confirms this. And the duration depends on how long the state of war lasts or a state of imminent threat of war. After that, the president of the republic, as we saw yesterday, is duty-bound to go back to the National Assembly to have this confirmed. And the National Assembly decides whether they will no longer be in force once the state of war is not there. But now they become enactments of the National Assembly, not of the president of the republic, and that's the way it remains in the future as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, as I said, we are going to move on to the relationship between the president of Serbia and other state organs, that is chapter 3 of your expert opinion, starting from 3.1 onwards. You saw already, in order to avoid repetition, I think that you have explained that in 238 through 313, or rather, 31 through 313 the relationship between the president and the National Assembly; namely, that the president does not have the right for legislative initiative and also that the Assembly can be dissolved only at an explained written proposal of the government, as stated in Article 89 of the constitution, that he only has the right to a seven-day suspension veto, that is Article 84 of the constitution. And also if the Assembly passes the same kind of regulation, nevertheless he has to promulgate it. I hope that you will agree with me that this is what your constitution is, that the rights of the president vis-a-vis the National Assembly are exceptionally limited?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. The president of the republic has minimal authority vis-a-vis the National Assembly. As a matter of fact, he is not the one that initiates elections for the National Assembly. He cannot even call sessions of the National Assembly. He doesn't have the right of legislative initiative either. He has only two rights. In relation to the promulgation of laws which is a declarative act, he has the right of suspension law veto; and we saw that that is for a very short period of time. And the consequence is that the vetoed law can be voted yet again with the same majority as in the first case, and then it's the duty of the president to promulgate that law. Also, the president of the republic can never follow this with initiative of his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. In the relationship between the president and the government, and it is the government that exclusively has executive powers according to the constitution, in paragraphs 314 to 320 of your expert opinion you refer to that. You will agree with me that the president has a subordinate position in relation to the government; namely, that some of his constitutional powers are limited by the fact that the government has to confirm certain things or restrict them. Namely, the president cannot carry out some of this without having obtained the opinion of the government beforehand.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. The president of the republic does not have constitutional powers vis-a-vis the government. We have seen that he can propose the prime minister designate, but as we've already said this is a decision that is imposed by the outcome of parliamentary elections. Once the government is constituted, he no longer has any authority over the government. He cannot chair government sessions. He does not sign government enactments. He himself cannot pass executive decrees. He cannot decide on the establishment and dissolution of government, ministries, and agencies. The only thing he can do is ask the government to present their position, or rather, his position on matters otherwise belonging to the jurisdiction of the government. As we said yesterday, by the very nature of this matter the president has the right to see what the government feels on certain issues that belong to their jurisdiction. However, the president cannot in any way express his dissatisfaction with the government views. He does -- he cannot impose any sanctions on the government. He cannot ask for a member of the government to be recalled or replaced. The government is really in close interplay with the National Assembly. The National Assembly chose the government, and the government is responsible to the National Assembly for its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, all of this is said already in your report. Can I ask you about Article 85. What's the purpose of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The purpose of this article is for the president of the republic to be informed of the work of the government or cabinet, and probably, as we saw from the relationship of the current president and the cabinet, to exert some kind of pressure on the cabinet, public pressure, for it to deal with certain issues. The public is informed about this. The president of the republic himself says that he asked the government or the cabinet to inform him on certain issues, and therefore he mobilises public opinion in order to get the government to hurry-up and deal with certain matters falling within its competence. That is the purpose of Article 85, nothing else. So the president has no powers. The president of the republic has no powers to influence the positions of the members of the cabinet while autonomous in their decisions, and they are responsible in political and legal terms to the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Is there any case law on the interpretation of Article 85 by a Constitutional Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you answer His Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there are -- there is no case law. The Constitutional Court of Serbia was handicapped in that. For a while it was not functioning properly, as it didn't have the correct number of judges. And even now in practical terms the Constitutional Court exists only on paper in the constitution because it has not been constituted yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, just a brief conclusion. If I understand correctly Article 85 of the constitution does not provide for or imply any kind of hierarchical relationship between the president of the republic and the government or cabinet; and the president of the republic, therefore, has no powers over the government, except for asking for information on the positions of the government?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Professor. Now, Mr. Zecevic, we are very appreciative of the fact that in representing Mr. Milutinovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- you have compiled a very restrictive list of witnesses and are focusing the defence very firmly on certain areas. However, even allowing for that and allowing for the very moderate way in which you appear to be presenting his defence, there are limits to how often you ought to be allowed to repeat what has just been said to us. We are conscious of the interests of everyone else. We've got to make maximum use of the time available. So please try to make -- in fact, please try not to repeat the very clear answers that the witness is giving.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, I think the best system might be to deal with examples. So please open tab 14, P1862, the Law on the Government, Article 19, please. Article 19 deals with the information that the government submits to the president under Article 85 of the constitution, and it states the following: "The deadline within which -- or the period within which the information is to be submitted shall be determined by the presidents, but as a rule it may not be shorter than 48 hours." If I understand it correctly - and please just tell me whether you agree with me or not - this 48-hour period is one that cannot be shorter, and it's there for the benefit of the government, not for the benefit of the president. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, that follows from the interpretation of the text of this article and the nature of things. The government has to study certain documents, for example, draw up its response, the relevant ministry within the sphere of whose competence the position falls, the position that the president of the republic is interested in, has to reply in writing so that 48 hours is a reasonable time for the government to prepare its response, to prepare its position, and present it to the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- The word "certain," "certain issues," is in this article and it's also in Article 85 of the constitution, and it seems in English an odd word to be in that role. Has it other -- has the Serb word other perhaps translations, such as "specific" or something of that nature? Or is "certain" the appropriate translation for that language?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The word in Serbian is "pojedina pitanja."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I then ask the -- well, if I may ask the interpreter if that can be translated in other ways than "certain"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Shall I spell the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: P-o-j-e-d-i-n-a p-i-t-a-n-j-a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's shown that way on the transcript. Can we have some assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It can mean "individual."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Individual is closer to specific and "specific" is what you would expect in this --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Specific issues. Yes. I think the most appropriate would be specific issues, specific questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can the interpreter comment on that, whether "specific" would be an appropriate translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It would be a possible translation, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, as the government exercises its executive power through the state administration, the position you put forward in your expert opinion, paragraphs 321 to 328, is that the president is cut off, so to speak, that's the term you use, from the state administration. In order to avoid repeating ourselves, could we please look at tab 15, P1823, the Law on State Administration, and then you can explain this position on a specific example.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation as regards the constitution is clear. The collective superior of the state administration is the government or the cabinet. It is the cabinet that has powers over the state administration. It appoints and relieves officials. It has personal power, also -- personnel power, also financial power over the state administration in that it proposes the budget for the National Assembly to vote on. Furthermore, the government or the cabinet monitors the work of the organs of state administration, ministries, and other organs of state administration, and exercising this function it can annul or render null and void certain enactments of the ministries and state administration if they are contrary to the law and other legislation so that the government can monitor. It can also organise. It has organisational power over the state administration in that by decree, and that is the only example of an autonomous constitutional decree, in the then-legal system of the Republic of Serbia, by a government decree it establishes the principles for the internal organisation of ministries and other organs of administration and special organisations. Therefore, the president of the republic has no special powers over the state administration. It is the government that has such powers, and these powers include personnel, control, financial, organisational powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Could you please open tab 46, P1737, the Republic of Serbia Law on Internal Affairs. Professor, could you please comment on Article 7 of the Law on Internal Affairs, please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 7 confirms the individual principle of the organisation of each ministry, including the Ministry of the Interior. The minister is the one who has all the powers of the ministry, and he prescribes the manner in which work in the ministry will be done and issues instructions in this respect. And this applies to each one of our ministries, including the Ministry of the Interior in accordance with the individual principle of the organisation of each ministry. So the minister is the one who has all the powers of the ministry vested in him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was -- this law was passed in 1991, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honours. It was passed in 1991. It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the legislature would make the law, the president would promulgate the law, and the government would act according to the law and the minister would, as a result, have a broad discretion in running his own department. Is it more complicated than that? Can you help me on that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, please comment on Article 9 of the Law on the Interior.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This article refers to a joint and simultaneous request of the National Assembly and the president of the republic to the minister of the interior. The National Assembly and the president of the republic may ask the minister to submit a report on the work of the Ministry of the Interior and on the security situation in the Republic of Serbia. At their request, he's duty-bound to submit such a report. This provision can be criticised, and I have criticised it in the course of my professional work because submitting a report to the National Assembly makes sense, as the National Assembly may, if it is dissatisfied with the minister's report raise the issue of lack of confidence in the minister in the Assembly, because it is the Assembly which appointed the minister. However, the president of the republic can in no way express his disagreement with the report. He cannot impose any sanctions on the minister. He cannot propose to the Assembly that the minister be dismissed. So it is not clear why the president of the republic is included in this article, why he together with the National Assembly may request a report on the work of the Ministry of the Interior. It's quite clear why the National Assembly can do that, but it's not clear why the president of the republic also does it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that information something that would not fall within Article 85 of the constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 85 requires, or rather, implies the position of the government or the cabinet on certain issues falling within its jurisdiction. Here it refers to the report of only one ministry, and the entire cabinet has nothing to do with that. It is the minister who submits such a report directly to the Assembly and the president of the republic. So it's not discussed at a cabinet meeting. The position of the cabinet, according to Article 85, is the position of the entire cabinet collectively. So it is adopted at a session of the cabinet and then forwarded to the president of the republic, whereas here there is direct communication between the president, or rather, the National Assembly and the president of the republic on the one side and the minister on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Minister of the interior, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the provision of Article 17 is one you have commented on in detail in your expert report in 329, so we will not go into it now to avoid repeating ourselves. It has to do with the decrees issued by the president when there is an irregular situation based on Article 83, paragraph 7 of the Constitution of Serbia. Professor, please let us now look at the law on the government, that is tab 16, or rather, the law on amendments, changes and amendments to the law on the republic or state administration, that's 1D376, and please comment on Article 2 of the Law on changes and amendments to the law on the state administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours -- Your Honours, Article 2 of the law on amendments to the law on state administration actually consists of under brackets Article 44(A). That is why the translation is only -- so it is the article of the amended law and this Article, 44(A), is added to the actual law on state administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I mean just for the translation purposes, to avoid any misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, would you please comment briefly upon Article 44(A), paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I have the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you just inquiring about paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, the entire article.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This article deals with the list of state administrators introducing the post of the deputy minister. Up until that time that position did not exist, the position of the deputy minister. There were only assistant ministers. This article now introduces this position, spells out his duties, says that deputy minister shall in the absence of minister replace him, that he's entitled to take part in cabinet sessions in the absence of the minister, and will have the same competence as the minister. And he may be designated to represent the cabinet in the National Assembly when laws or other regulations falling within the competence of the minister are debated. That means that he stands available to the National Assembly to give explanations on draft laws. This is something that normally only a minister is entitled to do, but here we see the deputy minister is entrusted with that as well. And then it says that the deputy minister shall be appointed by the cabinet for a period of up to four years, because it is never known whether a cabinet will have a term -- a full term of four years or not. It can always be voted out of confidence. At any rate, it says here that the deputy minister's term shall not exceed the term of the cabinet appointing him. So this article introduces the position of deputy minister which has not existed previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Just a brief digression tab 47, 1D413. This is the power of the National Assembly to appoint members of cabinet. Tab 47, 1D413 is the decision on -- to elect the deputy prime minister of the Republic of Serbia and minister of the interior in the Government of the Republic of Serbia, dated the 15th of April, 1997. Just a brief comment, please, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By way of this decision - and this is an individual enactment, by the way - so by way of this decision, the National Assembly in exercising its constitutional power elects the deputy prime minister of the Republic of Serbia and minister of the interior. The person elected at that time was simultaneously elected to the post of the deputy prime minister and that of the minister of the interior. This was done because, as I remember, both posts were vacant at the time because the deputy prime minister and minister of interior who had served prior to that were assigned other tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, is there always only one deputy prime minister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the constitution, there could be one or more deputy prime ministers. According to the 1990 constitution in practice, typically there were several deputy prime minister, and I'm not quite sure how many exactly there were up until 1994. But from 1994 until 2000, there were five deputy prime ministers. In Djindjic's government in 2001 I think there was six or seven deputy prime ministers, so even a greater number. It is not typical for a deputy prime minister to serve simultaneously as a minister, to head a ministry, it is not a typical situation. I think that this is a unique example under the 1990 constitution. I'm not quite sure of this, but I think that it is a sole example where a deputy prime minister simultaneously served as a minister as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Yesterday we discussed tab 23, which is 1D237 and P1015, the Law on the Ranks of Members of MUP. We said that subsequently this law was declared unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court. I would like to ask you for a comment, please, which you partially presented in paragraph 337 of your expert report. This has to do with the issue that a promotion to the rank of general does not automatically mean appointment to a certain position within the Ministry of the Interior, because that is done by a minister or in case of a state official, that is done by the cabinet, correct, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we have said so already. Appointment to a position when it comes to state officials falls under the jurisdiction of the cabinet, whereas appointment to all positions within a ministry falls under the jurisdiction of the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. When referring to appointment, we are referring to the duties that are to be carried out by that person. In order for somebody to be appointed, the rank of that person is not important, is not relevant at all, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the point of giving someone a rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me? Well, you know, I'm no expert for internal affairs, but a rank normally carries certain financial or other privileges. However, it does not automatically translate into a particular position. I'm not quite sure what privileges accompany a rank within the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but we've got to live in the real world here. If you promote somebody to general and therefore he gets a pay rise, you would expect he would have a job that merited that pay rise. Now, is that oversimplifying it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's a logical explanation. That follows the nature of things. Most likely that is how it is in practice. However, we also had assistant minister of the interior who held no rank, that was the case of Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have no difficulty with that whatsoever, Professor. What I have difficulty with is giving someone a title that gives them a large pay cheque and then suggesting that he will not be given some sort of responsibility that measures up to the pay cheque. Now, in the real world in Serbia, are there generals floating around the government with nothing to do getting large pay cheques from the Ministry of the Interior, or do you actually give them decent jobs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's not like they're not doing anything. We have a similar situation at the university. You can acquire a Ph.D. title, but that doesn't mean that you will automatically be appointed a lecturer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you don't automatically get paid for having an Ph.D. either. I'm trying to get a realistic appraisal of what happens in the real world in Serbia. This theory is all very real, but comparing generals who are being well-paid with Ph.D. graduates doesn't help us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was going to make a legal analogy. Those who acquire Ph.D. are given a supplement to their salary, and I think the same may apply to generals. But I'm not the right person to tell you about that. I'm no expert for internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that an explanation is due here. You said yourself that there existed a post of assistant minister who held that position without having a rank. You were referring to Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've just said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So that means that exercising powers and ranks are two completely separate things on the basis of that example. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in a certain situation, since the Trial Chamber would like to know how it looks in the real world in Serbia, after the change of power we had situations where some individuals in some ministries say in the Ministry of the Interior holding the rank of general continued to hold that rank, but did not have any tasks assigned to them that would carry powers. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that there were such situations in real world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness has already disqualified himself from answering that question because he says he's not got the necessary expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was just following your line of questioning. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, we have now completed the third chapter, the relationship between the president of the republic and other state organs. If the Trial Chamber has no questions concerning this portion, I would like to conclude this topic and move on to the next one. Thank you. Just a brief conclusion, Professor. In legal, scholarly literature, Serbia is not listed as a -- is not listed as a semi-legal country because the president of Serbia, according to the constitution --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Semi-presidential system, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I see the transcript -- semi-presidential system, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the president of Serbia, according to the constitution, does not have the powers that are typically held by presidents in such systems, semi-presidential systems?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the scholarly research, in the latest one also, Serbia is not listed as a country with semi-presidential systems. This type of government was established by the French constitutionalist, Maurice Duverger. So neither Duverger nor other authors dealing with that later qualified Serbia as a country with a semi-presidential system of government. France is one of the inceptors of such a system according to the constitution of the 5th Republic. This is so because in a semi-presidential system the constitution only deals with the mechanism for electing and recalling president of the republic. However, this very strict and demanding mechanism is not accompanied by appropriate powers. We have already dealt with the powers of the president of the republic. And if I may be said so, these powers remind me of Mihail Haynich from Austria who said that the only place where the president of the republic can stick his nose is his handkerchief. So practically speaking, he has no powers either to interfere in the work of other organs nor is he himself somebody who is vested with other types of powers, be it judicial, legislative, or executive. This is the reason why Serbia cannot be considered a country with a semi-presidential system of government. In my expert opinion I also quoted the Politika article of Misa Djurkovic, who in addition to being a researcher was for a while advisor to Mr. Kostunica, prime minister, who said himself that Serbia is not a country with a semi-presidential system, but it rather has a peculiar system of government which is typically in theory called the system of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the end of his sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the end of your sentence for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Serbia is not a country with a semi-presidential system of government, but has peculiar type of parliamentaryism defined as rationalised parliamentaryism in theory. This is a term introduced by French Professor Boris Mirkin-Gecevic. It was introduced between the two world wars this type of rationalisation of a classical British type of parliamentaryism came about. The countries with this system typically strengthened the position of the cabinet, and they are normally called countries with rationalised parliamentaryism.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know it's three minutes before the time we should break, but it is -- it would be appropriate at this point to break before I go into something else, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we finished with the question of the constitution now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. We are now moving to the question of a president's powers and competencies towards the army and the Constitution of FRY. We're going in that part. It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is his role as a member of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, 344 to -- paragraphs 344 to just -- to 361 of the expert opinion -- expert report of Professor Markovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As I explained yesterday, Professor, we have to break at this stage. We will resume at 11.15. Meanwhile, you should go with the usher and he will show you where you can wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just a question for the Professor, learned Professor, let's say if the president of Serbia had called you over a cup of tea and said, I want to use this handkerchief which is red in colour to show it to the bull to the state, how can I do it and can you help me constitutionally? What would be your reply, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand what this means. What is this bull of the state?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: You haven't been to the matadors ever? Have you ever seen the Spanish matadors? The president can sometimes act like that, and if he's a powerful president, he knows how to twist the arms. How would he do it? That's what we really we want to know from you as an expert.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I understood your question correctly, what he could have done is only what the constitution authorises him to do. But to twist arms on the basis of those powers, I doubt it. It's very small powers that are involved for him to be able to do something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, the powers that the president of Serbia has vis-a-vis the Army of Yugoslavia are exclusively derived from the federal constitution and his ex officio position as a member of the Supreme Defence Council. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is due to the fact that the Republic of Serbia does not have an army of its own. So the constitution could not have established that relationship between the president and the army. The federal constitution gave him this power ex officio, namely, by virtue of the position he holds he is automatically a member of the Supreme Defence Council. And generally speaking, the entire Supreme Defence Council is not an organ of that kind. All of its members are there ex officio. It is not that they were particularly elected or appointed members of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Please, tab 6, P856, actually, 1D139 is the translation, and that is the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Yesterday at one point you said that the powers, or rather, the authority of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia described in Article 77.7, I think it's under number 7. The defence and security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is solely within the realm of the state organs, isn't that right, the federal organs?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the competencies of the Federation are listed therein, and everything that is not on this list means that it falls within the province of work of the members of the Federation, the Republic of Serbia, the Republic of Montenegro, that they have powers vested therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, section 8 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia entitled "the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." Article 133, rather, states what the character and obligations of the Army of Yugoslavia are. So it is Article 133, paragraph 1. Could you please briefly comment on this. What is it that the army defends?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The functions of the Army of Yugoslavia are listed therein and it says that the Army of Yugoslavia protects four values from the point of view of the state and the constitution; namely, sovereignty, state territory, independence, and the constitutional order. The constitutional order is the order established by the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: From the point of view of this provision, Professor, if in a part of its territory and if in part of its territory, part of the Federal Republic Yugoslavia, there is an armed rebellion with the wish of that part of the state to secede, in your view would this constitute a threat to the constitutional order as referred to in Article 133 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No doubt that is what it would constitute, because everything that changes or wishes to change something by extra-constitutional means, that is to say apart from regular procedure, that is an attack on the constitutional order. The army by its function set in this article, Article 133, is duty-bound to defend the constitutional order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, tell me, these four objects that are defended by the constitution in Article 133, these are upper-most values of a state, aren't they, status values of a state. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No doubt. No doubt. Every state is a state because it has sovereignty, independence over a certain territory because it has organised authority within its territory. That gives it the attributes of a state, and those are precisely the attributes listed here that give a collective of individuals the properties of a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind what Article 133 states in its first paragraph, what is your opinion from the point of view of automatism in engaging the Army of Yugoslavia in case these four values are imperilled, those mentioned in this answer?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I did not quite understand what you were saying, my opinion about what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: About the automatism of engaging the army in cases when these constitutional values are threatened, or rather, all these things mentioned in Article 133.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 133 states this because this is an obligatory norm stated in the constitution. Therefore, the army is always called upon to defend this ex constitutio, sovereignty, territory, and the independence and the constitutional order of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, from that point of view then, no decision would be required of some other state organ for the army to be used in accordance with the constitution and the basic laws, that is to say the law on the army, in case these four objects are threatened?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no need for that because this is a constitutional duty of the army. I have already said this. I repeat, it is not necessary to do any such thing because this is a constitutional duty of the army that is derived from the supreme legal document of the country, and the army as an institution on the basis of the constitution is called upon to defend these four values or objects.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, please pause after I put my question so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be -- maybe I'm misunderstanding the purpose of these questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- but the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- the allegation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're not presumably suggesting that the army can decide whether there's a threat to sovereignty of the constitutional order and take action, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it cannot do so on its own. It can only be done by the organ set in the constitution. So this is what Article 135 of the constitution refers to. So it's not that it's going to act of its own accord. It has its own internal mechanism of organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I have to say I don't understand this, Mr. Zecevic. This will need to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, this is the question: Is it necessary -- let me be very concrete, very specific. Is it necessary to declare one of the irregular situations so that the army would defend on the basis of Article 133.1 the sovereignty, territory, independence, and constitutional order of the country, in your opinion? Is that indispensable? Is that the necessary course that has to be taken so that the president of the army -- the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia could issue such an order to the army, that it be used?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of Article 133, it is obvious that in every situation, be it regular, irregular, the army is called upon to defend the sovereignty, territory, independence, and constitutional order of the country. Therefore, it is not necessary to declare an emergency in order for the army to carry out this function. The army carries out this function by virtue of the fact that it is the army, and this is a characteristic vested in it by the constitution itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, have this sufficiently explained the issue or would you like me to pursue this? Could we -- I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. Well, my understanding at the moment is that without any other organ being involved, the army can itself act to defend the constitutional order on the basis that it thinks that there is some challenge being made to it, and I find that strange. If you feel you need to explore it further, it's a matter for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have 1D139, tab 6, P856 on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, on the basis of Article 135 which says: "In wartime and peacetime, the army shall be under the command of the president of the republic pursuant to decisions by the Supreme Defence Council," an order issued by the commander, by the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in accordance with the provisions of Article 135, paragraph 1 issued in peacetime when no irregular state was declared and when one of the four objects from Article 133 are under threat, is such an order to use the army in accordance with the constitution and the regulations of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It absolutely is, because it says in wartime and peacetime, so peacetime too. When the constitutional order is under threat, the army is therefore called upon to defend the country in this way. There are constitutions in the world where the army does not have all of these functions, where it only protects sovereignty and independence. But in this constitution of ours from 1992, it also defends the constitutional order, that is to say the order established by virtue of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind me, please, Mr. Zecevic, are there no provisions in this FRY constitution about declaring states of emergency or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- imminent threat of war?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are. The -- the constitution says that -- that the federal -- that the Assembly and the federal government are declaring a state of war and the other irregular -- irregular states --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which article is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just bear with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 78 and 90 -- 99 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 78.3 and 99.10. Your Honour, it is the -- it is the right of the National Assembly to declare one of the three states -- irregular states, but in case -- in case -- and that is provided for in Article 78.3, but in case -- yes -- Federal Assembly. But in case the Federal Assembly cannot meet, then the federal government, by virtue of Article 99.10, takes up these responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And where in the constitution are the consequences of such a determination set out?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I don't know if you can assist?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the constitution, but the Laws on Defence and on the Army of Yugoslavia that speak on this. The constitution regulates this only in principle, in the fundamentals, and the details are further elaborated in the laws and this law has almost 400 articles, and of course the regulations and other enactments issued pursuant to these laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I can be of assistance to the Trial Chamber, I believe Your Honour is looking for the Law on Defence, I believe Article 4. It is our tab 62, I'm told, 62, P985, Article 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can see that it's a question of degree, but I take it this goes to the question of how the army could be used and who could decide on its use in a particular way during 1998 and 1999. Or have you some other issue in mind here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, that's exactly what is the issue here. The allegation from the -- from my -- from the OTP -- Prosecutor's case was that the army was used in 1998 unconstitutionally. That is one of the allegations, that in order to use the army you should have declared one of the three states of -- one of the three irregular states, either a state of emergency, state of imminent threat of war, or state of war, in order to be able to use the army. Now, as Professor is saying in explaining the constitution, that is not the case. The army can be used under the command of the president of FRY, who commands the army in war and peace in -- according to the Article 35. So therefore, if the Commander-in-Chief or president of FRY gives a command to the army to deploy the army, in case one of the four objects are -- are at stake or are endangered, the four objects meaning the four objects from the Article 133 of the constitution, then this is completely in accordance with the constitution and the laws.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. I understand the point. You can move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just bear with me, Your Honour. I need to consult with my lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to just remind Your Honours that we have been presented during this case with the rules of engagement -- the Rules of Service Act of VJ, which is along the lines of what we are discussing right now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, let's go back.
