Article 135 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as we have stated here more than once, in paragraph 1 speaks about who commands the Army of Yugoslavia in peacetime and wartime, it's the president of the -- of the republic. And then it says who is in the Supreme Defence Council. And in paragraph 3, the president of the republic shall preside over the Supreme Defence Council. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are three separate issues, and each is regulated or provided for in a particular paragraph of this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I now wish to comment on Article 136 of the constitution, which provides for the powers of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. You spoke of this in paragraph 231 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 321, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- of your expert opinion, and you say that these are the exclusive powers of the president of the republic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the essence. A linguistic interpretation shows that the president of the republic exercises these powers independently, not in accordance with the decision of the Supreme Defence Council, but according to his own will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The powers you have just said that the president exercises independently according to his own will contain all the three dimensions of personal authority, appointing, dismissing, and promoting, three groups of persons that have to do with the Army of Yugoslavia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the president of the FRY appoints, dismisses, and promotes, quite independently, officers, judges, judge-jurors, and the prosecutors, military prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the persons in the Army of Yugoslavia or connected to the Army of Yugoslavia over whom the president has personnel power.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "personnel power," you mean personal power?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I mean in relation to issues of personnel and status, appointing, promoting, dismissing. When referring to officers, he can appoint and dismiss them. When referring to presiding judges, judges, and judge-jurors of military courts, he -- and he also appoints and dismisses military prosecutors. I'm not speaking of personal power, I'm speaking of issues of personnel, of staffing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the Supreme Defence Council as an organ was first provided for in the Constitution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia of 1992 for the period from 1945 onwards. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the first time such an organ which has only this property and no other was established by a Constitution of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just bear with me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, not the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The constitution I was referring to was the Constitution of FRY of 1992, not the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question, though, refers to 1945 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask the question once again. Maybe I wasn't ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Supreme Defence Council as an organ was first introduced in the constitutional practice on the territory of the former Yugoslavia from 1945 onwards in the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the first time in the constitutions of Yugoslavia, including the second Yugoslavia, the one that came into existence from 1945 to 1992, that such an organ was constituted which referred exclusively to the army and had no other function, apart from this function. That is the only time. Later on it was repeated in the constitutional charter of 2003, and now the constitution of 2006 has such an organ also.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in your opinion the reason why the Supreme Council is provided for as an organ in the constitution of FRY in 1992 is what, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I participated in drafting the constitution of 1992, I know the reasons first-hand. The reasons have to do with federalizing this state function of command of the Army of Yugoslavia. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was a so-called dual federation; it had the minimum number of federal units, only two. In the history of dual federations, they have always been short-lived, as can be seen, for example, in the example of Pakistan, of Czechoslovakia, and also the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In a dual federation, it is very difficult to achieve the equality of the two federal units. There will always be one which is dissatisfied because it does not hold a certain function. For example, there is a provision in the constitution of 1992, stating that the president of the federal government and the president of a republic cannot be from the same member state. And in order to federalize an important function in connection with the army, the Supreme Defence Council was established. Its members are not elected to that body. They're members of that body ex officio by virtue of their position; that's the president of the federal republic and the presidents of the two member republics. And in this way, the federal structure of a dual federation is best taken into account. Both federal units had their representatives in the Supreme Defence Council. So this was done to avoid discrimination in this important state function. That was the idea behind the Supreme Defence Council. That is the raison d'etre of this organ in the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's one part of your answer there I don't understand which says: "There's a provision in the constitution stating that the president of the federal government and the president of a republic cannot be from the same member state." That must be impossible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a provision of the constitution of 1992 -- just a moment. I find it hard to find my way through a copy of the constitution that is not mine, the one I normally use, but I'll find it right away. It's a provision of Article 97. It's paragraph 3 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which says: "As a rule, the president of the republic and the federal prime minister may not be from the same member republic." So as a rule --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but that's -- and that clarifies your answer. We can move on now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We have -- I was signalled by my colleagues that there is also a misinterpretation and -- in line 48 -- page 48, line 23, to 49, row 4, concerning the explanation given by the Professor, but I don't -- I mean, this would be the third time. The essence is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We know what you mean, I think, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time introduced in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, very briefly, please, yes or no. So this is the VCO, the Supreme Defence Council --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: VSO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is how it was designed, to symbolize the formal equality of these two member republics?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They wanted to ensure that in exercising this state function the two member republics would have equal status.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As for the source of the documents concerning the character of the Supreme Defence Council, we have this constitutional provision, we have basic laws, the Law on Defence and the Law on the Army. And we also have available to us minutes from the sessions where the words of the members of the Supreme Defence Council were recorded verbatim during the sessions. When preparing for your testimony here, you went over all of the minutes of the sessions of the Supreme Defence Council from the moment the late Slobodan Milosevic became president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in July of 1997 all the way up to the 9th Session of the Supreme Defence Council held on the 23rd of March, 1999, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, practically throughout the time-period during which Slobodan Milosevic served as the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While reviewing these minutes, you set aside three such minutes from sessions which are of particular interest, three or four of them, and we will be commenting on them now. The first one is the session of the Supreme Defence Council held on the 24th of November, 1998, this is tab 56, Exhibit P1576. Professor, tab 56, it's Exhibit 1576. It may be in the second binder.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These are the minutes from the 7th Session of the Supreme Defence Council held on the 24th of November, 1998, in Belgrade, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. So these are not shorthand notes, but rather minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Three members of the Supreme Defence Council were present, both presidents of the member republics, as well as the president of FRY who was also president of the Supreme Defence Council pursuant to Article 135, paragraph 3 of the constitution, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this is one of the rare occasions where other people were not invited, other persons were not invited to attend. Most often federal prime minister would attend these sessions as well as federal defence minister and Chief of General Staff. On this occasion, however, only members of the Supreme Defence Council attended as well as the secretary, who was also chief of military staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is the session of the Supreme Defence Council where they discussed the replacement of the then-Chief of General Staff, General Perisic. Would you please look at page 6, the comment of President Djukanovic, who was the president of Montenegro --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In English we only find five pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is page 4, the last paragraph, in the English text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, would you please give a comment of the words of President Djukanovic on page 5, second paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to that. The document is in evidence, it speaks for itself. He's an expert on constitutional law and not an expert on what Mr. Djukanovic said. I think it's inappropriate to proceed this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're trying to find out what is the character -- constitutional character of this -- of this body, VSO. So we are very limited with the sources. The only source, as I said, is constitution and the basic laws on -- Law on Defence and Law on VJ. But definitely I think important source would be the actual minutes of the -- of the VSO meetings. Professor will not be commenting on the actual content; he will comment on the understanding of the participants of the character of this meeting, which came out from their words in -- which are in the -- which are contained in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're talking about the last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm just putting in a context because President Djukanovic says that -- that he's opposing, and then President Milosevic is explaining to him the role of the president and of the Supreme Defence Council. And I think it's a very important issue, and Professor can comment on that from purely scientific point of view. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In light of what you've said, Mr. Zecevic, let's here the question phrased fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The way you've left it initially - admittedly you were interrupted - but it looked as though you were asking for a general comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that's not what we're hear to listen to. We can interpret this for ourselves. If you're wanting to put it in its context in some way, then we understand that line; but if all you're trying to do is ask what all this was about, then we can decide that on the basis of what's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Markovic, my question is as follows. Would you please comment from a purely scholarly point of view the content of these minutes, not just minutes from this particular session, but also others that we will be looking at. Would you please tell us something about the character of this organ as well as the character of decisions passed by this organ that we will see in minutes from some other sessions. I'm not asking you to comment upon the facts mentioned here because you were not present, and as His Honour has said the minutes speak for themselves.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These minutes - and I have read all of them - are quite valuable --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I have an objection to the form of this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is vague. The character of this body? What's he gleaned at from this is based on his review of all of the minutes. I think it's vague, it's non-specific, and I object to the form of the question. He's an expert on constitutional law. I don't see how this relates to his area of expertise, at least as the question is presently phrased.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my point is the following. If the decisions or whichever conclusions of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe we should have this discussion outside the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I agree, Your Honour, maybe the witness can be excused and we can resolve this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is -- well, my understanding is your question is about the way in which the Supreme Defence Council works.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And whether this illustrates it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it's two-fold, actually, not from this -- this concrete -- minute of this concrete session are aimed at how the VSO works, which I think is a very important issue for you to determine what is the character of that organ because that is the -- one of the issues which is in dispute. The other thing which is even more important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we can wait until you ask the question about that. Mr. Hannis, if that's what this is aimed at illustrating, then it appears to us to be within the competence of a constitutional expert to say that it appears to be operating either outwith or within the terms of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If the question is phrased that way, I don't have a problem, but as I see the question now it's an open question. It's a softball to him to say: Tell us about the character of this body. I mean, you yourselves, Your Honours, can see how this body worked by reviewing the minutes yourselves. You can see how it worked. His comment is about that isn't going to add anything to it that I can't add or anybody else in the courtroom can add. It speaks for itself. Now if the question is rephrased more along the lines that you described, then I'm probably going to sit down and shut up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, would you care to rephrase the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, would you be so kind and explain on the basis of your review of these minutes, what is your opinion as to whether this organ operated in accordance with the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; and if so, on the basis of what did you reach such a conclusion? And if your answer is negative, then what do you base that answer upon? Would you please help us with that, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These minutes are important because they clarify the meaning of Article 135, paragraph 1 of the constitution, especially this portion of this sentence: "In accordance with the decisions" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. Mr. Hannis now has a --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I apologise to the witness, Your Honour, but I think the question first was calling for a yes or no answer; and then once he gave his answer, yes or no, then he should explain why his answer was yes or no. We need to hear yes or no first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So, Professor, can you give us a yes or no answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, His Honour was referring to my question. Could you please give us a yes or no answer, could you assist us?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I can assist you, but I would rather interpret Article 135, paragraph 1, because it contains a certain notion: "In accordance with a decision" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, the -- there are actually two questions asked, and the first one is: What's your opinion as to whether the Supreme Defence Council operated in accordance with the constitution? Now, you can answer that either yes or no. Which answer would you wish to give?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And following on from that question, Mr. Zecevic wishes you to explain the basis on which you come to that conclusion from these minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your question quite well, Your Honour. When I said "no," I was referring to the fact that Article 135, paragraph 1, means that the Supreme Council adopts decisions, and there is a list of decision, just as there is a list of decisions of the president of the republic, the Federal Republic as supreme commander and Chief of General Staff. Those are rules, orders, instructions, and so on. Not a single enactment establishes the list of decisions that Supreme Defence Council can pass. I think that the word "decision" here was used in its generic sense without establishing the form of these decisions. However, if one goes through the minutes, one can see that the Supreme Defence Council did not pass any decisions; rather, they issued conclusions. All of the sessions that I reviewed in 1997 and 1998 and one session in 1999, nowhere did I find that the Supreme Defence Council adopted a decision. In only two of its sessions, one on the 9th of June, 1998, and the other one on the 4th of October, 1998, it passed conclusions. If one carefully reads those conclusions, one can see that they are no decisions. They are simply political views. And the president of the Supreme Defence Council interpreted Articles 135 and 133 [as interpreted] of the constitution in such a way that the Supreme Defence Council adopts conclusions and not decisions. This can be seen from this portion of the minutes that you're referring to now. This is how I interpret the words of President Djukanovic, president of Montenegro, as well. Now, as for the interpretation of these particular articles of the constitution, President Milosevic gave his interpretation of those articles on the same page of these minutes. By your leave I would refer to these portions, but when I said that my answer was no, what I was referring to is that the Supreme Defence Council never passed any decisions. No such decisions were published anywhere, in any kind of journal or gazette, not even in the military gazette or in the Official Gazette of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. There is no enactment establishing the form of such decisions, and if one goes over these minutes one can see that that body passed no decisions. They simply adopted conclusions which were of political nature, not of military or professional nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, am I allowed to pursue in this direction, Your Honour, or ... I'm wondering where we stand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, well -- I think the answer was given to a question that's within the area of expertise of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you can pursue that if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one intervention in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Whether one would agree with what he says about decisions and conclusions is quite another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. There is one intervention in the transcript in 58, 17, Article 135 and 136 I believe was the reference made by Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, when saying that the articles were interpreted, were you referring to 135 and 136 or 135 and 133?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in 136 the president of the republic carries out this independently, whereas in article 135 he does that in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, please tell me on the basis of responsibilities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia listed in Article 77 of the Constitution of FRY, paragraph 7, which says that it has competencies -- that it is only the federal republic that has competencies in the sphere of defence and security, then what is your opinion about the legal and constitutional position of the president of FRY in relation to the other two members of the Supreme Defence Council, that is to say presidents of member republics Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is certain that both in the constitutional and political sense, the position of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia carries greater weight. In the constitutional and legal sense, based on Article 135, paragraph 3, he's the president of the Supreme Defence Council. As for the political aspect, he was elected by a federal organ, by the Federal Assembly. He himself is a federal organ. By nature of his office, he has to have an overall picture and bear in mind the interests of the Federation as a whole, whereas presidents of member republics are limited only to the interests of their own republic. This is something that President Djukanovic stated explicitly in these minutes when he said that he was against the replacement of the Chief of General Staff, and he said, Not only am I against that, but I'm here conveying the position of the entire leadership of the republic. That is to say, he takes the viewpoint of his own republic, bearing in mind the interests of his republic, whereas the president of the federal republic has to bear in mind the interests of the federation as a whole. And it is for those reasons that his position carries greater weight, both in the constitutional and legal terms because constitution specified that he was the president of the Supreme Defence Council and also because he is a federal organ and has to bear in mind the interests of the federation as a whole, not just the interests of individual republics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, when it came to policy of the army, the use -- the policy of how the army might be used, the extent to which it might be involved in what would normally be seen as civilian affairs, if the president of the Federation took one view and the presidents of the two republics took the opposite view, what would be the power of the president as the commander of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course this is a hypothetical situation. The rules of procedure of the Supreme Defence Council regulate that, and these rules of procedure that were adopted I think in 1992 -- or was it 1993? I'm not sure. Well, they say that the Supreme Defence Council does not make decisions by consensus but by majority. That is to say that in that case it would be the presidents of the two respective member republics would prevail. However, my observation is that the Supreme Defence Council never made any decisions. It only adopted conclusions. That can best be seen if we were now to look at the conclusions of the session of the 9th of June, 1998, and the 4th of October, 1998. There is no decision there; there is just a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where do we see these?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- these are the tabs 54, P1574, it's 5th Session of the Supreme Defence Council, 9 June 1998, and that's at page 4 of the translation in bolded letters after: "Regarding this item of agenda FRY President Slobodan Milosevic proposed and the council anonymously adopted the following conclusions ..." And they're bolded, three conclusions. And the second one is tab 55, P1575, minutes of the 6th Session of the Supreme Defence Council, dated 4 October 1998, and the conclusion Professor had in view is listed on page 9, it's bolded and underlined, and it says: "Yugoslavia is in firm," I think "position" is missing in the translation, "in their choice of peace and ready to resolve all outstanding issues in a peaceful manner, but if we should be attacked we will defend our country with all means." Those are the two conclusions Professor was I think referring to, 9 June and 4 October.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, in the transcript of the 9th of June there are three conclusions, or rather, that is what President Milosevic proposed, three conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, will not these conclusions be in pari materia with the decision? I mean, only the word is "conclusion" being used because are you making too much of technical interpretation? Will not the word "conclusion" -- can anybody then differ with a conclusion, a conclusion reached at the defence council, can anybody amongst the three players differ with that conclusion, will it not be then a decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that these conclusions were supposed to be carried through by way of decisions yet to be reached. These conclusions are only political positions. To me they look like the positions of a party leadership, a party body, not of a state organ. So all these conclusions have to be turned into decisions that would operationalise these conclusions, otherwise they are merely political positions. In particular, these decisions would have to be published somewhere. I never saw any decision of the Supreme Defence Council. I never saw any decision of the Supreme Defence Council, and it seems that none even exist. Everything that exists is in the records, in the transcripts, and sorry that is not a legal document. It doesn't have any legal effect. All of this is contained in the transcripts, all of this cannot be singled out as a decision. It is an integral part of the transcript and that cannot yield any other result but political.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Of course, Professor, you can't change the nature of a dog by calling it a cat and albeit you may have a point to make about formality, in the end of the day we will be able to read these various statements and decide on their true nature. I can fully understand your comment in relation to the two that you've identified, but perhaps we'll hear more in cross-examination about others. I don't know. I haven't had a chance to explore this to ask you in detail about others, but I anticipate that from the Prosecution we'll hear more on that. Now is a suitable time to interrupt for lunch. Please go again with the usher, and we will see you back in court at 1.30 -- sorry -- yes, 1.30. Sorry, have I -- oh, sorry, sorry. I have -- yeah, I must be -- my mistake, Professor, we should go for another 15 minutes. I'm sorry. I have truly lost the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, let's please look at tab 57, P1000, that is a session of the Supreme Defence Council, one that was held on the 25th of December, 1998. On page 1 and on the last page -- I would be interested in hearing your positions on some of these matters. As for the English translation it's page 1 and then page number 10, the last two paragraphs that continue on page 11. In actual fact, Professor, we have seen that, as you said, Article 136 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, it is the exclusive autonomous right of the president of the FRY to appoint, promote, and recall officers of the army and so on and so forth. On page 1 of the minutes from the 8th Session of the Supreme Defence Council held on the 25th of December, 1998, there is an agenda, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is an agenda. It is interesting to look at the wording of item 3 on the agenda, since this is just information. It's no decision, no conclusion, it is merely information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So it's item 3: "Information on proposed appointments in the Yugoslav Army submitted for a decision to the president of the FR of Yugoslavia." If I understood you correctly, that is in full concord with Article 136 of the constitution because, as I've already said, that is the autonomous right -- I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The autonomous authority of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So this is not decided upon in accordance with the views of the Supreme Defence Council, but quite autonomously, as we've already said. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it's not clear at all why the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, who otherwise is the person who proposes agendas for meetings of the Supreme Defence Council, included this item on the agenda of the Supreme Defence Council meeting because he decides on this by himself without the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Would you please have a look now at the last page of this document, where the final positions are referred to. In the English text it is the last two paragraphs on page 10, and then pages -- on page 11 there are paragraphs 2 and 3. At the end here, or rather, in the text it says that: "At the end of the session President Milosevic presented and the Supreme Defence Council adopted the following final provisions."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Positions," interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the 8th Session of the Supreme Defence Council of 1998?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So I'm looking at the final positions, and point 3 reads as follows: "The Supreme Defence Council will continue to be apprised of all matters regarding the army."

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As in the minutes from the session held in November that we looked at a few moments ago in 1998, what was presented was an understanding, a view, of the role of the Supreme Defence Council; that is to say that the Supreme Defence Council is informed about matters pertaining to the Army of Yugoslavia. And in the minutes from November 1998, the president of the Supreme Defence Council expressed the same thoughts. And I am reading from that section. When concluding the discussion the president said that in the future as well he would always consult with the members of the Supreme Defence Council, the presidents of the member republics on the most important matters pertaining to the Army of Yugoslavia. This shows that the Supreme Defence Council is understood to be a consultative body, not a decision-making body. That is what was stated in the minutes from the 7th Session of the 24th of November, 1998, and we see here now in these minutes that you showed to me just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it you're -- that comment is confined to the personnel matters which were within the province of the president, and that he consulted the other two for the very reason you gave earlier about the involvement of the presidents of both republics to remove the suspicion of prejudice, so he took the very sensible view of consulting? Now, that's different from the previous article, which is talking about doing things in accordance with decisions of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it can be interpreted that way, too, although there is no linguistic material for that kind of interpretation. We can just assume that that is what the president of the republic thought, but he did not say that in so many words. Generally speaking, the Supreme Defence Council was inclined to include in its agenda matters that were not within its realm of work at all. And on the other hand not to make any decisions on matters that did fall into the province of its work. Most of the material from these sessions that I looked at from 1997 and 1998 and one from 1999 have to do with elements of the military budget. The military budget is a part of the federal budget. The proposed federal budget is put forth by the federal government, and it is the federal Assembly that adopts the budget. As for the federal budget, the Supreme Defence Council does not have any powers whatsoever. It should deal with matters pertaining to command over the army, because in Article 135 it says that the army is commanded by the president of the republic in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council. And the Supreme Defence Council is discussing material, financial issues that have to do with the budget, the selling of military property and so on and so forth. All of that can be seen from the agendas of its meetings held in 1997 and 1998. I did not read the minutes from the previous sessions held up until 1997. I don't know what the Supreme Defence Council dealt with then, but I myself was quite surprised that that is how the role of the Supreme Defence Council was interpreted. The constitution says something completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But there are constitutions where the -- the break-up of the budget to the army is something out of jurisdiction of the assemblies. They only give a consolidated budget or put it in a consolidated fund. And with respect to the various allocations, this is done a little privately. Maybe this is a role the supreme judicial council was assigned. Secondly, it also had a persuasive role, a role for instance, when it asked Montenegro to pay more than 10 per cent which it was paying, and Serbia was shouldering the 90 per cent of the budget. So those are sessions where such things could be discussed, it is not something in vain. That's what I feel, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I fully agree with you. Indeed there are such countries in the world, and then the Supreme Defence Council is the place that is supposed to deal with constitutional matters, including such a question, but that is not what this constitution says in Article 135. Otherwise, it is certain that the Supreme Defence Council is a place where elements of the military budget can be discussed, by all means. But that was not the concept of the constitution, at least that's the way I interpret it. In the previous period in accordance with the constitution of 1974, we had a Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which was a highest organ for command and control of the army, however this Presidency dealt with a great many other issues in addition to this one, whereas the Supreme Defence Council is focused on this particular issue. That is the only issue that, according to the constitution, this body should be dealing with. It doesn't have any other authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I note, Professor, that in tab 57 at the foot of the English page 9 and also at the top of page 10 it's plain that President Djukanovic thought that the Supreme Defence Council made decisions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot find that particular passage right now. I would appreciate it if I were told how this exactly reads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's in the debate in relation to the conduct of the Pristina Corps, and it all relates to the appointment of General Pavkovic to command the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, if I may be of assistance, it is page 13. It starts with the word "General Dragoljub Ojdanic" in bold, three pages from the end, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I haven't got pagination here. I don't have the pages numbered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the kind of document we have, so it is the third page from the end.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, the third page from the end, one, two, three.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The one-but-last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but what are these decisions of the Supreme Defence Council that President Djukanovic has in mind? Nowhere were any such decisions published. There are no such decisions. He probably means positions, positions, that's probably what he means because everybody says that positions are taken by the Supreme Defence Council. Positions are not decisions in a formal sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We have your position on that. It now is time to break for lunch. The usher will escort you as before, and we will resume at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.48 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [The witness takes the stand].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, analysing the questions and answers in the second half of this morning's session, I have come to the conclusion that it might be necessary for you to explain to us briefly the specification of enactments in the Yugoslav, or rather, Serbian legal system, if you can.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the classification goes like this. In the Serbian legal system you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time according to the constitution of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and also the federal legal system under the constitution of 1992.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly of the Federation enacted the constitution, laws, decisions, and conclusions. The federal government issued decrees, decisions, other types of decisions, instructions, and conclusions. The organs of state administration, that is the ministry enacted rules, orders, instructions, and decisions. The courts handed down judgements, these are individual acts, and the constitutional court issued decisions. The president of the republic issued ordinances. This same classification or specification or nomenclature was valid for the organs of the Republic of Serbia mutatis mutandis, that is, the National Assembly adopted a constitution but there had to be a constitutional referendum. Also, laws, decisions, conclusions, the president of the republic issued ordinances; the government issued decrees, decisions, other kinds of decisions; the ministry issued rules, orders, instructions, decisions, conclusions. The government would also issue guide-lines in the form of conclusions. The courts handed down judgements, whereas the Constitutional Court issued decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Out of that -- out of that list what I need to be clear about is what is a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me? I apologise. I don't know what Mr. Zecevic's intention was with this question, but one has to conclude that the names, the nomenclature of these legal enactments were provided for by the constitution or the laws. For example, the Law on the Government established what enactments the government could issue. This we also see in the Constitution of Serbia in Article 90. The Law on State Administration provided for the types of documents issued by the ministries. The Law on the Army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I follow that, Professor. It's the word"conclusion," the category that you call a "conclusion" is one I'm completely unfamiliar with. I'd like to know what a conclusion is. Give me some examples if that would help.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can give you examples. For example, the conclusions of the National Assembly before the state delegation went to Rambouillet and on the delegation's return to Rambouillet, those conclusions were issued by the National Assembly. I don't know what number it is here. I could show you what these conclusions looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's a part of the factual binders which we have not distributed, but it will be probably tomorrow and then we can show the form of the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. I shall wait till then, Mr. Zecevic. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just add --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just add that a conclusion is not a legal enactment. A conclusion expresses the positions of the organs issuing the conclusions about a certain issue or matter falling within the competence of that organ. So they do not represent legal norms; they simply express the positions of the relevant organs about such and such a question. But they are included in the list of types of documents and their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Do you think you -- is this the same word for "resolution" you are trying to use or "resolution" will be different than "conclusions"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how this word has been translated. Decision is a legal act with a legal norm, with legal force, unlike a conclusion which has no legal force. It only expresses the standpoint on a certain issue. A conclusion is binding only in political and moral terms, but not in terms of legal sanctions, whereas a decision, a "resenje," carries legal sanctions with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you satisfied, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: No, it's okay, it's a question of language. I think I'm familiar with the word for this type of activity as a resolution, like the Security Council passes a resolution and the General Assembly passes a resolution, they are resolutions. And then if these are conclusions, or he's taking them at power of a conclusion, that's another thing. We understand what's a decision, what's an adjudicatory decision or otherwise, and an order also.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you explain in relation to a resolution of the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, conclusions are similar to resolutions, they are similar. A resolution also expresses a standpoint on a certain issue falling within the competence of the body issuing the resolution, and the same goes for conclusions. Conclusions are not legal enactments and they are not worded in the manner of legal documents with numbers of articles and paragraphs and so on. So that even in appearance, not only in content, conclusions differ from legal enactments such as laws, decrees, decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Professor, this nomenclature which was in force in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia is not specific to Serbia alone. In comparative law are there other states in Europe with similar nomenclatures of legal enactments?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. All over the world the parliament has a representative body, passes laws, decides on amendments to the constitution, now there are systems in which governments can issue decree laws but this possibility never existed in our country to have decrees law -- decree laws issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Let's briefly go back to tab 54, P1574. These -- this is a conclusion issued at a session of the Supreme Defence Council held on the 9th of June in paragraph 2, article 2, paragraph 2. Have you found it, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a translation into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And please look at page 4, it's in bold. What I'm interested in is the following. This conclusion is in the conditional form. If something happens, as a consequence of that something else will happen.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The conclusion says if the terrorist activities of the Albanian separatist movement escalate, the Yugoslav Army will intervene adequately. This is the question I raised before the break. How on the basis of such a conclusion, we might even call it a decision, can one command the Army of Yugoslavia? What does the word "adequately" means here? It's not explained in operational terms, in operative terms. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, without going into the substance of the matter, but looking at it from the legal aspect purely, such a conclusion in order to be operational would have to have some subconclusions adduced to it or another decision where it would be established that certain conditions have been fulfilled, and then adequate intervention would have to be defined. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I think that this is simply a political position which must be developed further with an expert decision. So based on this position, a decision would have to be issued which would not be expressed in these generalised terms which are not in compliance with legal language.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at tab 55, P1575. These are minutes of a session, the 6th Session, that is, of the Supreme Defence Council of the 4th October -- 4th of October, 1998. And the conclusion I have in mind now is on the page before last of the text in Serbian, or rather, on page 9 of the translation. This conclusion, like the previous one of the 9th of June, is also in the form of a conditional sentence. It says if something happens, then the country will be defended with all means. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, likewise. The language of this is the language of a political position. It is yet to be operationalised. One cannot command on the basis of this conclusion. What does it mean is firm in their choice of peace ready to solve all outstanding issues in a peaceful manner? This does not relate directly to the Army of Yugoslavia, it's got nothing to do with commanding, it's a political position. And if we should be attacked, we will defend our country with all means. Well one such means is the Army of Yugoslavia, but what are all these means? This is to be further developed in a decision operationalising and implementing this political conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. To illustrate this we will show what kinds of enactments are issued by the organs competent to deal with military matters in the broad sense of the word, and we will show that each of these enactments has a particular form which is prescribed. Please look at tab 63. This is P984, the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, on the armed forces. Have you found it, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: First let's comment on Article 4, which states -- and I'm actually interested in the last sentence. The article lists eight points establishing what the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia who commands in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, as can be seen in the constitutional text, what the president does when commanding. So he establishes the principles, determines the system, decides on the deployment of the army, and also approves the plan for the use of the army, and so on and so forth. And then the last point says or the last line: "In performing the duties described," that's command duties, "the president of the republic shall issue orders, commands, and decisions." So the Law on the Army as the basic legislation for the use of the constitutional provisions of Articles 133, 134, 135, and 136, and primarily the two last of these, prescribes precisely the particular types of documents issued by individual organs in relation to military matters and also the form these enactments are to take or documents. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Anyone who knows how to read this can see that from this article, and it says here that the president of the republic, or rather, the president of the Supreme Defence Council is not primus inter pares. He is also independent, he also has independent powers and these are all listed here. And everything he does is done in the form of legal enactments and these are orders, commands, and decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Two matters arising out of that. First of all, whether he can do anything set out in this article on his own will depend on whether it's constitutional to do so. Is that correct, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It stems from paragraph 1, that he does all of these things in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, and then in commanding the army he has the following possibilities; they are enumerated in eight items, these possibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All in accordance with decisions of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, but what I said is that I have never seen a decision of the Supreme Defence Council, nor do I know of any that exists. I only saw conclusions of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The second matter is this, the last paragraph that you were referred to which says: "In performing the duties described in paragraph 2 the president shall issue orders, commands, and decisions ..." And you say that that's paragraph 2 above, which is "determining the system of command in the army." Does it follow that in exercising the powers under 1 and 3 to 8 the president can't issue orders, commands, and decisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that all of these matters, all of these duties listed in eight items, the president of the republic carries out these duties by issuing a particular enactment. Nothing can be done without an enactment because it is only through an enactment that a legal obligation arises. He can issue commands, orders, or decisions, and it says also here under item 6 that he can issue basic rules or regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you assist me then with a possible explanation of why paragraph 2 is singled out in the last sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have a correct text of the Law on the Army, it has a total of two paragraphs. The first paragraph has eight items, and the second paragraph is what you just mentioned. And this must be a mistake. So either it should say from item 2 of paragraph 1, I think that's how it should read because the text that I have has a total of two paragraphs. But the first paragraph has eight items or eight subparagraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have on the screen, please, the B/C/S version of that paragraph -- of Article 4. And then the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it possible that the reference is not to item 2 but actually a reference back to Article 2 of the organisation -- of the law itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, unless I'm overcome by fatigue, all I see in Article 4 are two paragraphs, a total of two paragraphs. And in my view, I don't know if others have a different text, but the text that I have has a total of two paragraphs. And the second paragraph says what you just read out in -- I think that this is a mistake, that it should read: "In paragraph 1 herein" -- or if they wanted to single out just item 2, then they should have said: "Paragraph 1, item 2 ..." that's how it should have been worded. It's not clear to me because paragraph 2 is mentioned in the very paragraph 2, in the same paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I take it we have as official a copy of this proclamation as we could have --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Definitely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's the Official Gazette of -- number 43 of 1994 dated 27 May 1994, and this is a P exhibit which both parties stipulated to. It is official text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: If I might with the leave of the Presiding Judge. Professor Markovic, I must confess that on a first reading of the last paragraph of Article 4, I had believed that the distinction was in respect of paragraph 2, to -- the duty to determine the system of command in the army and oversee its implementation. The distinction was is that there was a specific duty in relation to that duty, whereas in all the other instances in that article it were merely discretionary. Is that a possibility? In that particular paragraph, paragraph 2, there is a specific duty based on the last sentence, whereas in all of the other cases there is no duty but there must be a discretion depending on the circumstances of it, particular duty. Are you understanding me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I fully understand that, but I think that a duty is contained in all of these items. Say item 4, it says here that he has to regulate and order measures. How is he going to order measures unless he issues orders? I don't know whether later on there came a corrigendum in later editions of the Official Gazette. Perhaps there was a corrigendum there, but it is obvious here that this article has a total of two paragraphs and paragraph 2 refers to itself, to the very paragraph 2. So it's either a mistake, either it should have read item 2 of the first paragraph of paragraph 1. Because there are typos, you know, they do occur in Official Gazettes, but later on normally a corrigendum is issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, I will attempt to find the corrigendum this afternoon. This is the first time that I came across that myself, but would you please look at Article 6.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which in a way explains this mistake in Article 4. Article 6 says: "In order to implement enactments issued by the president of the republic and the duties of commanding the army, as well as the duties stipulated by this law, the Chief of General Staff shall issue rules, orders, commands, instructions, and other documents." So here the enactments issued by the Chief of the General Staff are enumerated in cases where he implements enactments issued by the president of the republic. And all of these enumerated enactments have a predetermined specified form, don't they?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We have an entire nomenclature of enactments here. We have rules, orders, commands, instructions, and other enactments. So each of these enactments has a specified legal form.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if we were to take the position that this was a typo in article 4, which we will verify and inform the Trial Chamber of, the president would be entitled to issue orders, commands, and decisions, so specific types of enactments, and none of the articles or other regulations specify the form of the enactments issued by the Supreme Defence Council, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It is not specified either in the Law on Defence or the Law on the Army. They say nothing about the types of enactments issued by the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: By nature of things, these documents -- by nature of things, these documents would have to be - if I can say so - of a lower rank, lower level, because according to the constitution the president commands in accordance with. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and what is most important is that they need to be published because the constitution explicitly sets forth that all regulations need to be published. The Constitutional Court - and at the time I was a judge of that court myself - took the position that a regulation which has not been published is not a regulation and cannot be assessed for its constitutionality and legality. That was the position taken by the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia back in 1991. I'm quite certain of that because I was a judge of that court at that time. So a regulation that has not been published is not a regulation. It simply does not exist in a legal world, and there is no document specifying what the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, and they have not been published anywhere. And the constitution explicitly says that whatever has not been published is not a regulation at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in order for the rule ignorantia legis nocet which means that ignorance of law does not excuse one -- the regulation needs to be published. Furthermore, one cannot be held responsible, or rather, the president of the republic cannot be held responsible for violating the constitution if he were to command without the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council because we don't know at all whether the Supreme Defence Council has issued any decisions and where these decisions were published. So according to the 1992 constitution, the president of the republic could command even without the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council without violating the constitution. Why? Because we have no such decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, and we do not know whether he commanded in accordance with those decisions or not and who formulated those decisions, we don't know that either. As the Trial Chamber probably knows, the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is held responsible for violating the constitution, and the first president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Dobrica Cosic, was recalled by the Assembly because the Assembly believed that he had violated the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, it may be your position is different from that of the witness, I'm not entirely clear, because you've stressed that these implementation orders must be of an inferior nature because the president has to command the army in accordance with decisions of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But as we understand the witness's position, it is that no such decisions were ever made, but nevertheless the president could do as he pleased without the authority of the Supreme Defence Council. In other words, they were a sort of brake only. They didn't do anything positive, but they could intervene to brake, or put the brakes on what he was doing. That's how I understand what he's saying, otherwise these words don't have any meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a theoretical aspect. I said by nature of things it should be that the orders by way of which the president commands in some sense represent an inferior enactment, because these orders have to be in compliance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where do we find these decisions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where do we find these decisions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the whole point, Your Honour. The decisions are not existing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, maybe they were never written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, according to the Professor, then they are not existent in a legal sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But still somehow or the other the president still has power to command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, according to the Law on VJ, he has the power to command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So these words don't actually have any significance. You can ignore the words: "In accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council ..." and read this without them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in practice it would look like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, now let us move on very briefly, please, to the rights of the members of the Supreme Defence Council. The constitution does not mention this nor does any other formal regulation. The only regulation that could seem relevant in this respect is an internal enactment of the Supreme Defence Council itself, the rules of the Supreme Defence Council. So far there were three of them: One from 1992, 1999, and 2001, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tab 59, P2622, is the 1992 rules of procedure?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one did you say?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, it is important to observe here that these rules of procedure were never published in an Official Gazette or similar publication. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is [as interpreted]. In the legal world it does not exist until it is published. So this was only an internal document of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think we have a problem with the transcript, 84, 21. The answer was: "Yes, it is not." It hasn't been published. Maybe it's my problem, the way how I pose the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, was this document published somewhere or wasn't it -- was it not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document to the best of my knowledge was not published, and the first time I saw it was when preparing for this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The same applies to the rules of procedure of 1999?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With respect to what you said just a while ago about the Constitutional Court, as this was never published the court could never evaluate its constitutionality and legality?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. If a regulation or rules have not been published, objectively they do not exist, they are not materialised in the legal world. So the Constitutional Court lacks the elements on the basis of which to evaluate the constitutionality of the document. The regulation or the rules of 1999 contain very -- contain a provision that goes completely against the constitution, it violates the constitution, but there was never any basis for the Constitutional Court to rule on it. It -- it actually provides for something that is already provided for in the constitution, but it does so in a different way, in a way that's completely opposed to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I wonder if you might be able to find for us for tomorrow the decision of the Constitutional Court dealing with the matter, the one that the witness has been referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Definitely, Your Honour, I will give the instruction right now. Just let me confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to assist ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I assist, Your Honours. I wish to assist the Defence. The Constitutional Court adopted this position about an enactment of the Presidency of the SFRY in 1991, and it refused to evaluate the constitutionality of that document because it had never been published anywhere. The decisions of the Constitutional Court are published in the Official Gazette. It was the Official Gazette of the SFRY at the time, and this was in the year 1991 and had to do with evaluating the constitutionality of an enactment of the Presidency of the SFRY and it also referred to command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Can you kindly give us, if you can, the reasons for non-publication. What could be? Was it a design or was it inadvertence or this was not followed. Do you have any information or knowledge or your own views about it? We would like to hear, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My opinion is quite simple. I think the rules were not published because they had not been drafted by the Supreme Defence Council. The Supreme Defence Council only adopted political positions which were yet to be formulated as decisions. And secondly, the Supreme Defence Council was not an expert legal organ capable of issuing such documents, and there were people in it without any military education or training. So how could they issue legal decisions concerning commanding of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But, Professor, the rules that our attention has been drawn to are signed by the president and stamped with the official stamp. And Judge Chowhan is asking why when all these formalities have been carried out would the document not be published in the gazette.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can only speculate about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please do not speculate. Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, we are talking about tab 59, P2622. Would you kindly comment on Articles 4, 5 -- or 4 and 5. After that we will comment on Article 7, but first let's start with Article 4 about convening the sessions of the Supreme Council?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 4 is clear. It's always the president who convenes a session, and he can do so on his own initiative or at the proposal of a member of the Supreme Defence Council. It doesn't say he is duty-bound to convene a session if a member of the Supreme Council proposes it. The formulation is such that he may or may not convene a session in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So one of the two members of the Supreme Defence Council, according to this, would have the right only to propose to the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, who according to the constitution is also the president of the Supreme Defence Council, to convene a session of the Supreme Defence Council. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. He can only propose that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia who is, according to the constitution, also the president of the Supreme Defence Council has the discretionary right to decide whether to accept this or not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The formulation is such that this interpretation is possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at Article 5. This article deals with the agenda for the sessions. The agenda is also put forward or proposed by the president of the Supreme Defence Council or the chairman, but a member of the Supreme Council may also propose an agenda. So the idea is the same as in Article 4, a member can only propose or suggest?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same formulation, but reading the minutes I have never seen an instance of a member of the Supreme Defence Council proposing an amendment to the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, according to our usual practice, if there was a duty or an obligation on the president to convene or -- well, to convene a session or include an item on the agenda at the proposal of one of the members of the Supreme Defence Council, these provisions would have been worded quite differently, would they not? They would have been worded explicitly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: An example of this would be the Constitution of Serbia, P855, tab number 5, Article 79, paragraph 3 or item 3. Can you explain this very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's tab number 5, P855.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have that on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, what article?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 79, paragraph 3. This article refers to an extraordinary session of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the wording is such and that it says the National Assembly shall convene on an extraordinary session upon the demand of not less than one-third of the total number of deputies or on the demand of the government with an agenda prepared in advance. So the Assembly shall convene if one-third of the deputies demands that or the government. The president or the Speaker of the National Assembly does not have the discretionary right to decide whether or not to convene an extraordinary session. An extraordinary session must be convened ipso facto because at least a third of the deputies have requested it or of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you Professor. Let us go back to the Law on the Army. Yes, the Law on the Army, tab 63, P984. Professor, we have seen Article 4 concerning the powers of the president of the republic as the commander of the army and the other organs of the General Staff and so on. Is it not a fact that in the Law on the Army, except for paragraph 1 of Article 135 which contains a provision from, or rather, in Article 4, paragraph 1, which actually has the same text as Article 135, paragraph 1 of the constitution, there is no further mention of defence [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can assert that with confidence because I think I have read the entire law carefully, and I think that this is the only place where the Supreme Defence Council is mentioned. It's a long law and it has 366 articles, so it's three times longer than the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have a correction in the transcript, 90, row 6: "No further mention of the..." It says here "defence," it was "Supreme Defence Council." After the "no further mention of Supreme Defence Council."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, let's look at the following. When analysing the Law on the Army, let's look at chapter 13 which refers to the responsibility of members of the military and disciplinary responsibility first of all. That's on page 39 of the English translation, and it's Article 159. Professor, Article 159 distinguishes between different kinds of disciplinary infractions. There is an error and an offence or an infraction and an offence, a less serious and a more serious form --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of military discipline. Yes. It draws the distinction of disciplinary -- breaches of discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Article 168 on the following page authorises the president of the republic - this of course refers to the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia - to lower, mitigate, or pardon every disciplinary measure or sentence, does it not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He has the right to pardon disciplinary breaches.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, a brief comment on Article 173, the Rules on Military Discipline.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just let me take a look. We can see here what enactments can be issued by the president of the republic. These are the rules on military discipline and in the nomenclature of enactments rules are also mentioned. So the president of the republic can issue rules, and he has only procedural authority here; namely, to prescribe the procedure and jurisdiction for disciplinary offences and who has the right to impose disciplinary measures and sentences, whereas the offences themselves are regulated by the law. So here he has procedural authority, and the law prescribes the substantive rules. So the procedural matters are regulated by the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say substantive norms, you are referring to -- when you say substantive norm, you are referring to Article 159 which we have mentioned, you are referring to the norm from that article?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just see.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
