utterances.text: Let me just see. 160 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was referring to 159, which establishes the kinds of disciplinary breaches.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but disciplinary breaches are regulated, specified by the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And now, please, Article 204, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This deals with the responsibility during a state of war. Would you please comment on paragraph 3 of Article 204.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here he's given a power that he does not have under normal circumstances, the power to prescribe other disciplinary measures or sentences other than those stipulated by the law or prescribed by the law. Or he can rule that certain disciplinary measures or sentences established by that law will not be applied. So he can either introduce new ones or he can decide that some of those prescribed by the law will no longer be used; that is to say he can modify the provisions of the law when it comes to certain disciplinary measures or sentences. In addition to that, he can also prescribe different procedure and jurisdiction for reviewing these matters as well as different rules for the responsibility of service members and establish different organisation operation of military disciplinary courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, would you agree with me that Article 204 regulates a situation where there is a state of war, during which time the powers of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia are expanded in relation to the powers he has in peacetime when it comes to the discipline of the members of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His powers are expanded in those circumstances. He's even authorised to amend provisions of a law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Professor, on the basis of these documents, or rather, now that we're dealing with the Law on the Army, let us look at some other articles as well, please. Article 46, please, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Exceptional promotion. By way of this article, the president may exceptionally promote a professional officer to the rank of general?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the proposal of the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes this is the same power as the one mentioned in Article 136.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this is an exceptional promotion; that's where the distinction lies, I think?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, and this exceptional promotion can be done at the proposal of the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the proposal of the president of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the basis of the constitution, and its Article 136 has the power to promote under regular circumstances generals, to remove them, to appoint them, and so on, whereas by way of this article he can also implement an exceptional promotion on the basis of this Article 46 of the Law on the Army?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Article 107, Professor -- just a moment, please. I think it's paragraph 6. I'm tired myself now, but I think it's paragraph 6 of Article 107 that speaks of a situation where a professional officer -- and then under item 1 it says that the president of the republic may keep in service a professional officer --

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the rank of general.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this article established the basis for termination of professional service ex lege by operation of law, but it also created a possibility whereby president of the republic may keep in service a professional officer even though conditions for terminating the service have been met. A professional officer who holds the rank of general, even though that particular person has met the conditions for retirement, as stipulated by law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now the final article is 151, chapter 12. Authority to decide on service relations and issue of other enactments. Where it says that the president and then it speaks of four powers of the president. Do you see that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the president promotes two initial ranks to the ranks of major-general or higher, and then he also issues decisions on transfers, service status, admission to professional service, and termination of service. And he also appoints officers with the rank of colonel to duties for which the rank of general has been determined in the establishment. If I understand this well, Professor, these powers enumerated in Article 151 give absolutely all existing powers to the president of the Federal Republic when it comes to appointment, transfer of officers, their promotion?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This article is a way to partially make more concrete Article 136 of the constitution because Article 136 of the constitution says that the president appoints, dismisses, or promotes officers mentioned in the federal law, and then the federal law in the first two items specifies which officers of the Army of Yugoslavia those are who can be appointed, promoted, or dismissed by the president of the republic. And then the law goes on further saying that the president of the republic also issued decisions on transfer, service status, admission to professional military service, and termination of service of generals. And then in item 4 it says that he appoints officers with the rank of colonel to duties for which the rank of general has been determined in the establishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hope this is leading somewhere, Mr. Zecevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- because we can read all these provisions for ourselves, and you can make submissions about them. So is there a point on which we need an opinion here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, one of the basic laws for implementing the constitution when it comes to the army is the Law on the Army, that is the most concrete, basic law, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Everything that is related to the authority over the army, that is to say commanding, appointments, promotions, dismissals, transfers, disciplinary procedures, fall exclusively under the jurisdiction of the president of Yugoslavia, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except for Article 4, which we have mentioned already, where the tasks from Article 4 are something that he conducts in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which is mentioned in Article 135?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Article 135, whereas all other responsibilities that you have just mentioned, they arise on the basis of specific provisions of the law, and the president of the republic conducts them independently without the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, Professor, on the basis of the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia that we have just analysed, members of the Supreme Defence Council, do they have any independent authority in relation to the Army of Yugoslavia in your view?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They have none. They only have authority as members of that body, collective body, where the decision-making goes either by majority of votes or as the rules of procedure specify -- but the rules of procedure were never applied, but they still specify that it can be done by consensus. So they have no independent authority; they only have authority as members of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But even as members of the Supreme Defence Council, on the basis of Article 136 of the constitution, they have no power to relieve of duty, to recall, or to transfer any member of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They do not have such authority. It is only the president of the republic that has such authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The same pertains to the ability of the members of the Supreme Defence Council as a collective body to punish or to hand down a disciplinary measure in relation to any member of the armed forces or the Army of Yugoslavia on the basis of the provisions of the Law on the Army that we have just analysed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We have explained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, now that we are here I would like to comment upon the constitutional text, or rather, I would like us to draw a parallel between the provisions of Article 135 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, where it says that the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia commands the Army of Yugoslavia in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council. So between that and the formulation that existed in the Constitution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, which is tab 9 here, and it's P1623, Article 313, paragraph 3, and Article 328, paragraph 2. So the constitution from 1992 only uses the term "command," and this is something that the president does in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council under Article 135. If we look at the Constitution of the SFRY, Article 313, paragraph 3, it says here: "The SFRY Presidency is the supreme body in charge of the command and control of the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in war and in peace." Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on this formulation, it is completely clear that the Presidency of the SFRY is a supreme collective body. So it is the highest, that is to say the supreme body in charge of command and control of the armed forces of the SFRY in war and peace. No such qualification is given in relation to the Supreme Defence Council. It is not stated anywhere that the Supreme Defence Council is the highest organ of command and control of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So that means that that would be one distinction, and the other one if you agree has to do with control. In the 1992 constitution it says that the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia commands in accordance with in war and peace, whereas it says here that the Presidency is the highest organ of command and control. Professor, I'm not asking you to explain to us what it means to control the armed forces - it's not part of your expertise - I'm just asking for you to confirm that there is this distinction between two constitutional texts.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, basic reading implies that. These are two different qualifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And I think that there is another very important distinction between the provisions of the 1992 FRY constitution, Article 135, that we have quoted several times here, and Article 328 of the Constitution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia of 1974, paragraph 2 of that article where it says that: "The president of the Presidency of the SFRY shall, on behalf of the SFRY Presidency, carry out command of the armed forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia in compliance with the present constitution and federal law." Professor, would you please explain the difference between this situation described in Article 328 of the SFRY constitution, paragraph 2, where it says that the president commands on behalf or in the name of, so what's the difference between that and the text of Article 135 of the 1992 constitution?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The formulation of the 1974 constitution, Article 328, paragraph 2, firmly links the president of the Presidency to the decision relating to the command of the armed forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. He, the president of the Presidency, commands the armed forces only on behalf of the Presidency. But the Presidency is the one who made the decision. It is quite clear. But since the Presidency is a collective body comprising eight members, it is a physical impossibility to have all eight of them commanding the army. No. They make the decision, and then on behalf of that body, the president of the Presidency commands the armed forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. In the 1992 constitution, it says that the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia commands the Army of Yugoslavia pursuant to decisions of the Supreme Defence Council. So it's not on behalf of the Supreme Defence Council, but rather in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council. This is a much weaker link, and based on the minutes from the sessions we can see that this Supreme Defence Council adopted decisions in the form of conclusions. So the president commanded the army in accordance with those conclusions or positions. So there was a much weaker link between him and the Supreme Defence Council and their decisions. There was a much weaker link than the one existing between the president of the Presidency and the Presidency of the SFRY. The presidents of the -- the president of the Presidency was himself a member of the Presidency; he wasn't a separate individual organ, as is the president of the republic, who is only an ex officio member of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please, Professor, just slow down a little for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I have to repeat anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, it's all right, but please try to speak a little more slowly. I know it's late. We'll be finished quite soon. Professor, you said that the Presidency, the eight-member Presidency was a collective organ, a collegium. According to the provision we have just read out, the president of the Presidency commanded on behalf of or in the name of that organ, and that's stated in the constitution. On the other hand, in 1992 again we have a collegium, a three-member organ, a collective organ. So the difference between three and eight is only in the number of members, nothing else; isn't that correct? But in this case in the constitutional text it is not stated that the president commands on behalf of or in the name of the Supreme Defence Council. It just says in compliance with or pursuant to decisions. But would you agree with me my conclusion that based on analysis of these two decisions we can conclude that the Presidency as a collegial organ, a collective organ was the organ that had command and control over the armed forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, whereas in 1992 the VSO, the Supreme Defence Council, did not have that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. First of all, it's a leading question, although that's not such an important issue with expert evidence. But secondly, it goes to an important issue for us to determine. The Professor has explained how he sees the differences between the two constitutional -- sorry, the two army rule and constitutional provisions, and we shall take that into account in determining the very matter that you have raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, let's just analyse very briefly tab 62, the Law on Defence, P985. Professor, the Law on Defence is, I would say, of a more general character than the Law on the Armed Forces, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it speaks of defence in general, not a single subject of defence as the Law on the Army does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In Article 2 lists the subject who have rights and duties in the defence of the country, among them the Army of Yugoslavia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After that as lex specialis we have the Law on the Army which we have already analysed and which relates only to the Army of Yugoslavia. Is that correct, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's a special law, the Law on the Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in chapter 4 there is a list of the state organs which have certain functions in defence, those are Articles 40 to 48. The Law on Defence as the umbrella legislation further develops the constitutional provisions of Articles 133, 135, and 136. Is that correct, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you see that under the rights and duties of state organs, the Law on Defence draws a distinction between the president of the republic under 1 and the Supreme Defence Council under 2, although as we have seen in the constitution, the Supreme Defence Council is collective three-member body consisting of that same person, the president of the FRY, who is by virtue of the constitution the president of the Supreme Defence Council, and the other two members are the presidents of both member republics. What is your opinion as to why this distinction has been drawn so that the rights and duties of the president of the republic are provided for in one article and he is an organ playing a role in the defence of the country, while the rights and duties of another organ, the Supreme Defence Council, in the defence of the country, the president being a member of that, are provided for in another article? Can you illuminate us or at least comment on these provisions of the Law on Defence, Articles 40 and 41?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this entire chapter deals with the rights and duties of state organs, and this refers, of course, to the rights and duties in the defence of the country of particular state organs which are established here. And in view of the way Article 135 of the constitution is formulated, it is not quite clear why in this law the president of the republic is separated out. He should not really exist here, apart from this Supreme Defence Council, because whatever he does he does pursuant to the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council. To be sure, that is actually explicitly stated in the first and only paragraph of Article 40, that in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council the president of the republic does, and then there is a list of what he does, whereas in Article 41 there is a list of the tasks carried out by the Supreme Defence Council with reference to defence. So the intention of the legislator is unknown to me here. I don't know why the legislator has decided to distinguish between these two institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Professor, Article 41 which defines the role of the Supreme Defence Council sets out eight things for which it is responsible and then says: "The president shall ensure implementation of the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council," and that looks as though the Supreme Defence Council are expected to make decisions in relation to the eight items listed. In your researches, have you found no decisions of the Supreme Defence Council made in relation to these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never found any decisions, apart from the conclusions in the minutes from the sessions of the Supreme Defence Council or the stenographic records of these sessions. I have never seen a decision entitled "Decision of the Supreme Defence Council" with a text following underneath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And remind me over what period of time have you researched this? What period do your researches cover?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My research covers the period in which the president of the FRY, who was also of course the president of the Supreme Defence Council, was Slobodan Milosevic. That is from July 1997 to September 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're -- we will be moving to another direction, so I think it's proper that we break here for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In which direction shall we be moving?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, very shortly we have a PowerPoint presentation number 3 which will -- which will explain the terminology on Supreme Command, supreme commander, staff of the Supreme Command, and similar. And we have a brief -- we briefly are going to touch upon the certain laws for -- in between 1989 and 1998 which are relevant to this case, but very -- and to the limited scale of presentation and of very limited number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that would conclude the expert role of our distinguished Professor here, and then we're having of course the factual part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That then, Professor, brings our proceedings to an end for today. Please bear in mind tonight and every other night that you're here what I said yesterday about not discussing the evidence with anyone. You may leave the courtroom now with the usher, and we'll see you again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 8th day of August, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.28 p.m.,
